content: Low levels of zinc in the blood have been proposed as a potential factor contributing to adverse pregnancy outcomes. These outcomes may include prolonged labor, uterine atony leading to postpartum hemorrhage, pregnancy-induced hypertension, preterm labor, and post-term pregnancies. However, these associations have not been definitively established. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of zinc supplementation during pregnancy on maternal, fetal, neonatal, and infant outcomes. Specifically, it compared outcomes in healthy pregnant women who received zinc supplementation versus those who did not or received a placebo. Additionally, the review sought to assess these outcomes in women who were zinc-deficient or likely to be zinc-deficient. To update the evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth’s Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, as of July 3, 2020. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included, and studies had to involve zinc supplementation initiated before 27 weeks of gestation. Quasi-randomized trials were excluded. Studies presented only as abstracts were considered if sufficient information was available or could be obtained from the authors, though no such studies were identified. The review included 25 RCTs involving over 18,000 women and their infants. The overall risk of bias was low in approximately half of the studies. The findings suggest that zinc supplementation during pregnancy may have little to no effect on reducing the risk of preterm births (risk ratio [RR] 0.87, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.74 to 1.03; low-certainty evidence). Similarly, zinc supplementation appears to have little to no effect on reducing the risk of stillbirth (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.88; low-certainty evidence) or perinatal deaths (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.51; low-certainty evidence). The evidence regarding the effect of zinc supplementation on neonatal death is very uncertain due to the very low certainty of the data. Regarding other birth outcomes, zinc supplementation likely has little to no effect on mean birthweight (mean difference [MD] 13.83 grams, 95% CI -15.81 to 43.46; low-certainty evidence). It probably also has little to no effect on reducing the risk of low birthweight (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.13; moderate-certainty evidence) or the risk of small-for-gestational-age infants (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.12; moderate-certainty evidence) when compared to placebo or no supplementation. Subgroup analyses were not conducted because very few studies included populations with normal zinc levels. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to support the notion that zinc supplementation during pregnancy improves maternal or neonatal outcomes. Future research should prioritize strategies to enhance the overall nutritional status of pregnant women, particularly in low-income regions, rather than focusing solely on zinc supplementation.
